teaser: A Last Supper where the table runs off at an angle and the lamp smoke turns into angels.
review_notes:
Canvas size about 365 x 568 cm.
The idea that the oblique table was planned for viewers who see the canvas from the side, on the right wall of the chancel, is a common scholarly reading, not a documented intention.
Workshop participation (son Domenico) is generally accepted but its extent is debated.
Judas identified as the haloless figure in red on the near side of the table: standard identification.
Studio motto 'the drawing of Michelangelo and the coloring of Titian' is reported by his 17th-century biographer Ridolfi.
Companion canvas on the opposite wall: The Jews in the Desert (Gathering of Manna).

lesson.text: Take a boat across the water from St. Mark's Square in Venice and you land on a small island with one great white church: San Giorgio Maggiore. Benedictine monks have lived here for about a thousand years. Walk up the bright nave to the main altar, turn your head to the right, and this dark, crowded canvas hangs above you. It has never left.

The church was designed by Andrea Palladio, the architect of calm: pale stone, tall columns, daylight everywhere. In the early 1590s the monks asked Jacopo Tintoretto, then in his seventies, for two huge canvases to face each other across the altar. Into Palladio's quiet white box he brought a night scene full of smoke.
“Tintoretto” means “the little dyer.” His father dyed cloth for a living, a big trade in a city famous for its silks, and the nickname stuck to the son for life.

The subject is the last meal Jesus shares with his twelve followers, the apostles, before his arrest. A century earlier, in Milan, Leonardo da Vinci had painted the version everyone knows: a long table set straight across the picture, Jesus exactly in the middle, everything balanced. Tintoretto knew that model well. See what he does to the table.
Three lines show how the picture is built, and what it refuses to do.

lines.label: Leonardo's table
lines.text: This is where tradition would put the table: flat across, facing you like a stage. Everyone visible, everyone in a row, the main figure at the center.

lines.label: Tintoretto's table
lines.text: Instead the table rushes away from the lower left into the depth of the room. The apostles shrink as they go back, and Jesus ends up small, far along the cloth.

lines.label: The path of light
lines.text: A second diagonal crosses the first. It drops from the hanging lamp to the glowing head of Jesus, then down to the servants working in the foreground.

lesson.text: So the most important person in the room is neither the biggest nor the closest. You find him because of light. In this dark tavern there are only two sources of it: an oil lamp, and the people themselves. Each apostle's head gives off a thin halo, a ring of light that painters use to mark a holy figure. One halo burns far stronger than the rest.
Tintoretto replaces balance with movement. A table set on a diagonal and a light that jumps from point to point pull your eye through the room instead of letting it rest.

There is a practical reason too, some historians think. The canvas hangs on a side wall, so the faithful walking toward the altar see it at an angle. From there the table seems to continue the real space of the church, as if the supper were being served a few steps away.

The canvas is about 3.65 meters high and 5.7 meters wide (roughly 12 by 19 feet). Tintoretto was famous in Venice for working fast. In one well-known contest, his rivals handed in sketches, and he is said to have turned up with the finished painting already installed.

Speed shows in the paint. Up close, many shapes are made of a few fast strokes of pale color dragged over a dark ground. Nowhere is that clearer than in the air above the table, where something strange is happening to the smoke.

lesson.title: Where the light comes from
lesson.text: Follow the light from the ceiling down to the table.

spots.title: The lamp
spots.text: A hanging oil lamp flares with two flames. Its smoke curls outward in pale ribbons, and the ribbons start to grow arms and wings.

spots.title: Angels of smoke
spots.text: On the right the smoke has become a flight of angels, drawn in see-through white strokes. You can still read the ceiling beams behind their bodies.

spots.title: Jesus
spots.text: He stands and leans toward an apostle, bread in hand. His halo is the brightest thing in the room, a burst of rays against the dark.

spots.title: The one without light
spots.text: Alone on the near side of the table sits a man in red with no halo at all. This is Judas, who will betray Jesus that same night.

lesson.text: Notice what Jesus is doing. In Leonardo's picture he has just announced that one of the twelve will betray him, and the scene is all shock. Here he is feeding an apostle a piece of bread. Tintoretto paints the first Communion, the rite in which Christians share bread and wine as the body and blood of Christ.

That choice had weight in 1594. Protestant churches in northern Europe had broken with Rome, and one of the fiercest quarrels was over what Communion really means. Catholic churches answered with images. Hung beside the altar where monks performed the rite every day, this canvas says: what happens here began at that table.

And yet half the picture belongs to people who are not paying attention. The whole right foreground is a kitchen. Servants carry dishes, a woman kneels over a basket, fruit is piled on a side table. The holy meal takes place inside an ordinary, noisy Venetian inn. One guest in that kitchen is not even human.
An animal has come to see what is in the basket. Where is it?

spots.title: The cat
spots.text: A tawny cat stands on its hind legs and peers over the rim of the wicker basket while the kneeling servant reaches in. It cares about dinner, not miracles.

lesson.text: The cat, the baskets, the glass wine flasks on the cloth: these everyday things make the miracle easier to believe, because the room is so familiar. Painters of the next generation, in the style we call Baroque, would build whole careers on this mix of deep shadow, sudden light and plain people.
According to an early biographer, Tintoretto kept a motto on his studio wall: the drawing of Michelangelo and the coloring of Titian. He wanted the muscle of one and the rich paint of the other.

He delivered the canvas in 1594 and died on May 31 of that year, aged about 75. Assistants from his workshop, including his son Domenico, likely helped with a job this size. But the idea is his, and it is one of the last things he gave his city: a supper lit from inside, still hanging by the altar it was painted for.

quiz.question: Where does this painting hang?
options: In the church of San Giorgio Maggiore, beside the altar
quiz.explanation: It was painted for the island church of San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice and has never left.

quiz.question: How does Tintoretto place the table?
options: On a diagonal running into the depth of the room
Flat across the picture, like Leonardo
quiz.explanation: The table rushes away from the lower left, so the figures shrink with distance.

quiz.question: What are the angels in the upper part made of?
options: See-through white strokes, like lamp smoke
quiz.explanation: The smoke of the oil lamp seems to turn into transparent angels.

quiz.question: How can you recognize Judas?
options: He sits alone on the near side, without a halo
He stands next to the lamp
quiz.explanation: He is the man in red on the viewer's side of the table, the only apostle with no light around his head.

quiz.question: What moment of the meal is shown?
options: Jesus giving bread to an apostle, the first Communion
quiz.explanation: Tintoretto paints the sharing of bread, the rite performed at the altar next to the canvas.

facts.text: Tintoretto's nickname comes from his father's trade as a cloth dyer.
In this picture Jesus is the largest figure, placed at the front of the scene.
facts.explanation: He is small and far along the table, found thanks to his bright halo.

facts.text: Tintoretto painted this canvas as a young man at the start of his career.
facts.explanation: He was in his seventies and died in 1594, the year it was finished.
